df["Score"].plot(kind="hist",bins=(30),color="purple")
plt.ylabel("No_of_Students")
plt.xlabel("Score")
plt.title("Score Distribution")
plt.show()
In [ ]:
## 1. Insight

1.	Scores cluster at 41-50 (31 students) and 81-90 (27 students) — two distinct 
    groups indicating moderate academic performance. 
2.	37 students (18.5%) scored below 40. The minimum score of 30 may indicate 
    an assessment ceiling effect
3.	A small percentage of students achieve exceptionally high scores, 
    reflecting academic excellence. 
4.	Introduce remedial learning programs also, improve teaching methodologies and expand 
    student mentoring initiatives.

In [4]:
df.groupby("Course")["Score"].mean().sort_values().plot(kind="bar",color="Black")
plt.ylabel("Average_Score")
plt.title("Average Score By Course")
plt.show()
In [ ]:
## 3. Insight

1.	Maths has a high average score (65.0) foloowed by ICT and Economics respectively 
    but the lowest pass rate (64.3%), suggesting an uneven spread — a few high scorers 
    inflate the average while many students fail.  
2.  Science has both the lowest mean score (59.4) and a below-average pass rate 
    (71.4%), pointing to systemic curriculum or teaching challenges. 
3.	Course complexity significantly affects student outcomes. 
4.  Commission a curriculum audit for Science, invest in practical/laboratory 
    equipment, and improve teacher professional development with an expansion 
    in digital learning resources.

## 4. Insight
1.	Students studying 1–9 hours daily show similar score distributions, pointing to ineffective study habits
    or poor learning environments.
2.	High scorers (90+) are scattered across all study-hour brackets, suggesting quality of study matters more than quantity.
3.	This challenges the assumption that extending school hours or homework will improve outcomes.
4.	Introduce study-skills training and Encourage balanced study schedules.

## 6. Insight

1.	Male and female students perform nearly identically — average scores differ by only
   1.0 point (99.0 vs 98.0), this indicates a gender-equitable learning environment.
2.	Despite males scoring marginally higher on average, females may
    have a slightly higher pass rate, suggesting females may be more consistent near 
    the pass threshold.

4.	Neither gender significantly dominates the top 10 performers, with a 6M–4F split.
5.  Conduct qualitative surveys on student experience by gender and 
    establish gender-responsive pedagogy training for all teachers.

df['Pass_Status'] = np.where(df['Pass_Status'] == 'Pass', 1, 0)
course_pass_rate = df.groupby('Course')["Pass_Status"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False) * 100

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
course_pass_rate.plot(kind='bar', color='skyblue')
plt.title('Pass Rate by Course (%)')
plt.ylabel('Pass Percentage')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('3_pass_rate_by_course.png')
plt.show()
In [ ]:
## 11. Insight

1.	English has the highest pass rate at 75.8%, while ICT lags at 64.3% — the lowest of all courses.
2.	Only English and Math meet or exceed the 75% pass threshold; all other courses fall short.
3.	ICT's low pass rate despite significant study hours signals curriculum or assessment misalignment.
4.	Economics, the most enrolled course (43 students), has only a 67.4% pass rate — a serious systemic concern.
5.	Difficult subjects require stronger academic support including an improvement in 
    teaching techniques and increase practical learning opportunities.

In [44]:
numeric_cols =['Age', 'Score', 'Attendance', 'Study_Hours']
correlation_matrix = df[numeric_cols].corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
sn.heatmap(correlation_matrix, annot=True, cmap='coolwarm', fmt=".2f", vmin=-1, vmax=1, ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Correlation Matrix of Numerical Metrics')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('4_correlation_matrix.png')
plt.show()
In [ ]:
## 15. Insight

1.	All correlations (Score–Attendance: 0.036; Score–Study Hours: –0.050; Score–Age: –0.074) are near zero, 
    indicating no single factor drives performance in isolation.
2.	The near-zero correlations suggest unmeasured variables (teacher quality, parental education, school resources) 
    are the true drivers.
3.	The slightly negative Score–Age correlation (–0.074) hints that older students marginally 
    underperform — worth investigating.
4.	The Attendance–Study Hours negative correlation (–0.112) suggests students who attend more classes
    study less at home, possibly trusting class instruction.
5.	There should be a serious development of data-driven education policies, including 
    strengthening of academic intervention programs  and expand educational 
    analytics adoption.
In [13]:
df_chronological = df.sort_values('Student_ID').reset_index(drop=True)
df_chronological['Rolling_Score_Avg'] = df_chronological['Score'].rolling(window=15, min_periods=1).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(df_chronological.index, df_chronological['Rolling_Score_Avg'], color='purple', linewidth=2, label='15-Student Moving Avg')
ax.set_title('Score Trend (Proxy: Ordered Student Records)')
ax.set_xlabel('Sequence of Enrolled Students')
ax.set_ylabel('Score (Rolling Average)')
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('5_score_trend_over_time.png')
plt.show()
In [ ]:
## 16. Insight

1.  Grouping students sequentially reveals avg score fluctuations between 58 and 67, 
    indicating intake quality, seasonal factors, or assessment timing influence results	
2.	Academic performance improve and decline across periods and also long-term
    trends indicate institutional effectiveness. 
3.	The flat performance trend over the cohort suggests no evidence of learning acceleration from early to later students.
4.	Educational interventions influence score progression. 
5.	Introduce early academic intervention systems and monitor academic trends continuously
    including, the expansion of teacher's development programs.
In [56]:
Q1 = df['Score'].quantile(0.25)
Q3 = df['Score'].quantile(0.75)
IQR = Q3 - Q1
lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

outliers = df[(df['Score'] < lower_bound) | (df['Score'] > upper_bound)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
sn.boxplot(x=df['Score'], color='lightcoral', ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Boxplot for Score Outlier Detection')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('6_score_outliers.png')
plt.show()
In [ ]:
## 17. Insight

1.	No statistical outliers detected via IQR method (Q1=45.75, Q3=81.25, IQR=35.5).
    Score variance is high but organically distributed.   
2.	Outliers help identify gifted or struggling students. 
3.	Score anomalies may reveal examination irregularities and Outlier detection 
    improves educational monitoring. 
4.	Strengthen academic integrity policies and improve student counselling services.
